The faucet snail Bithynia tentaculata exhibits a life cycle tightly coupled to freshwater environments, with several key size thresholds defining its ontogeny. Newly hatched individuals emerge from egg masses with a shell height of approximately 0.12 cm [Lb = approximately 0.12 cm], a diminutive size that nonetheless marks the beginning of an independent exotrophic existence. These neonates graze on periphyton and detritus, growing rapidly until they reach a settlement phase, defined by a shell height of 0.121 cm . This latter measurement, nearly indistinguishable from the birth size, reflects a very brief pelagic or crawling larval period before the snail firmly establishes itself on the substratum. The time elapsed from hatching to this settlement event is approximately 3 days after hatching , underscoring the rapid transition to a benthic existence. Field surveys of populations in the Great Lakes region indicate that the maximum, or ultimate, shell length attained by adults is 1.1 cm [Li = 1.1 cm], a modest dimension that places this species among the smaller members of the Bithyniidae family in North America. This ultimate length is rarely achieved outside of stable, food-rich habitats such as macrophyte beds in nutrient-rich lakes.

Reproductive maturation in Bithynia tentaculata is size-dependent rather than strictly age-dependent, with females initiating gametogenesis upon reaching a specific morphological threshold. Puberty, defined by the onset of egg production, is triggered when a female attains a shell height of 0.7 cm [Lp = 0.7 cm]. Snails below this size, regardless of their chronological age, remain reproductively inactive, directing all available energy toward somatic growth. Once this size benchmark is surpassed, the snail enters a reproductive phase that can last for several seasons under favorable conditions. The onset of egg mass deposition is a notable event in the life history, as females must allocate considerable resources to produce the gelatinous clutches that are attached to hard substrates like stones or aquatic vegetation. Monitoring of marked individuals has confirmed that the transition from juvenile to reproductive adult is sharp, with gravid females first appearing in the population only after surpassing this critical size threshold. Under laboratory rearing conditions, females attain this puberty size approximately 60 days after hatching [tp = 60 days after hatching], providing a temporal as well as a morphological marker for sexual maturation.

Reproductive output in this species has been quantified under controlled laboratory conditions, particularly at a constant water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. At this temperature, females produce eggs at their maximum reproductive rate, which is realized through a combination of clutch size and spawning frequency. Detailed observations show that a single female deposits approximately 23 eggs per egg mass [N_R_i = approximately 23 eggs per egg mass], a moderate fecundity for a prosobranch snail of this body size. Furthermore, these spawning events occur with a frequency of about one egg mass every 365 days [Ri = about one egg mass every 365 days]. This combined output constitutes a total annual fecundity of 23 eggs per female per year [Ri = 23 eggs per female per year], enabling a modest but sustained recruitment to the population. The synchrony of this reproductive rhythm with the thermal regime ensures that hatchlings emerge during periods of peak algal productivity in late spring and early summer.

Biomass allocation in Bithynia tentaculata provides insights into its energetic strategy, particularly in relation to the shell and somatic tissue. For an individual with a shell length of 6 mm, the dry mass of the soft body parts (flesh) alone averages 0.00525 grams . This minute value underscores the snail's relatively low investment in somatic tissue compared to the shell, which constitutes a significantly larger fraction of the total wet mass. The complete animal, including its calcareous shell, weighs approximately 21 mg at this same size, meaning the fleshy component accounts for only about one-quarter of the total mass. Such an allocation pattern is typical for aquatic gastropods inhabiting environments with high predation pressure from shell-crushing fishes or crayfish, where a robust, thick shell provides a critical defensive advantage. This morphological investment in protection thus directly influences the snail's energy budget and its ability to allocate resources to growth and reproduction over its lifespan.

Longevity in Bithynia tentaculata has been best characterized under stable, predator-free laboratory conditions maintained at a constant temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. Under these ideal circumstances, the maximum recorded lifespan is approximately 4 years [am = approximately 4 years] at a temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. This duration, while modest compared to some larger freshwater mollusks, is considerable for a gastropod of this small body size, reflecting a generally slow life-history pace punctuated by seasonal reproductive bouts. In natural settings, actual lifespan is likely shorter due to predation, parasitism by trematodes, and environmental stressors such as winter hypoxia or summer desiccation events in shallow water bodies. Nonetheless, the four-year potential lifespan provides a valuable baseline for demographic models, suggesting that a single cohort can overlap with several others, contributing to sustained population densities in favorable habitats. This extended reproductive window allows females several opportunities to breed across multiple seasons, with the capacity to produce clutches annually for up to four consecutive years under optimal conditions.
